newsitem.title: UK: Mining giant RTZ-CRA still upbeat despite profits fall.
newsitem.headline: Mining giant RTZ-CRA still upbeat despite profits fall.

text.p: RTZ-CRA, the world's biggest mining company, reported a 24 percent drop in 1996 profits Thursday, but soothed investors' sentiment with upbeat comments over its near-term prospects.

The British-Australian company said net profit after tax fell to $1.1 billion in 1996 from $1.4 billion in 1995 following sharply lower metal prices and operational problems with its Kennecott copper smelter in Utah.
Adverse exchange rates were an additional factor behind the fall, which was widely expected, the company said.
If anything, industry watchers took heart from upbeat comments from RTZ-CRA, which said it that higher production volumes and a lower effective tax rate would underpin its 1997 performance.
"I expect our growth to continue at a rate in advance of the market overall," chairman Robert Wilson said.
RTZ-CRA, formed through a merger late in 1995, also announced that it plans to change its name to Rio Tinto, to help create a clear identity.
"It is highly desirable to have a single identity rather than the confusing image stemming from the double acronym," Wilson said.
RTZ-CRA suffered from a 22 percent drop in copper prices in 1996 and a 16 percent fall in aluminium following the trading scandal triggered by Sumitomo trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
"We do expect the tightness is going to ease, maybe not this year, but perhaps as we go into 1998," Wilson said.
The price drop last year depressed profits by $311 million, while technical hitches at its flagship Kennecott smelter cost the mining giant about $150 million.
Adverse currency movements shaved another $38 million off the 1996 results.
